proofs.proof_tex:
Put \(x=\sqrt N\).  By the rate bounds and rate membership,
\[
 a(p)=\frac{\lambda}{\lambda+\tau+\nu}\geq \frac{c}{3C}\geq\beta,
 \qquad
 1-a(p)=\frac{\tau+\nu}{\lambda+\tau+\nu}
 \geq \frac{2c}{C+2c}\geq\beta .
\]
The positive root of \(\beta x^2-Gx-1=0\) is
\(r=(G+\sqrt{G^2+4\beta})/(2\beta)\).  The definition of \(N_0\) and the
assumption \(N\geq N_0\) imply \(x\geq r\), hence
\[
 \beta N-G\sqrt N\geq1.
\]
Using \(|\gamma|\leq G\) gives
\[
 Na(p)+\gamma\sqrt N\geq \beta N-G\sqrt N\geq1
\]
and
\[
 Na(p)+\gamma\sqrt N
 \leq N(1-\beta)+G\sqrt N
 =N-\{\beta N-G\sqrt N\}\leq N-1.
\]
Taking ceilings preserves both integer bounds, proving the claim uniformly.

Write \(\delta=N^{-1/2}\).  All constants below depend only on
\((c,C,G)\); this convention is legitimate by the rate bounds, rate
membership, and staffing window.  The staffing-interior lemma makes every
birth and death rate used below an interior finite-chain rate.

For the treatment arm, put \(x=(k-Na)/\sqrt N\) and
\(g=\gamma_N\).  Since
\(M_N=Na+\sqrt N g\) and
\(\lambda(1-a)=(\tau+\nu)a=q\), direct substitution in the treatment
generator gives the exact scaled drift and local second characteristic
\[
 \delta\{\lambda(N-k)-\tau k-\nu\min(k,M_N)\}
   =-dx-\nu\min(x,g)=:b_g(x),                                      \tag{1}
\]
and
\[
 \delta^2\{\lambda(N-k)+\tau k+\nu\min(k,M_N)\}
 =2q+\delta\{(\tau-\lambda)x+\nu\min(x,g)\}.                       \tag{2}
\]
For the control arm the corresponding formulas are \(-dx\) and
\(2q_0+\delta(\tau-\lambda)x\).  Taylor's formula for
\(f\in C_c^3(\mathbb R)\), applied only to jumps whose rates are nonzero,
therefore proves, for every fixed \(R_{\mathrm{loc}}\),
\[
 \sup_{E_{0,N}\cap[-R_{\mathrm{loc}},R_{\mathrm{loc}}]}
 |(G_{0,N}-\mathcal L_0)f|+
 \sup_{E_{1,N}\cap[-R_{\mathrm{loc}},R_{\mathrm{loc}}]}
 |(G_{1,N}-\mathcal L_g)f|\leq C_f\delta.                         \tag{3}
\]
The ceiling identity gives \(0\leq g-\gamma<\delta\), so (3) is the
asserted generator convergence.

We next establish stationary tightness uniformly.  For the treatment chain,
(1)--(2) give
\[
 G_{1,N}x^2=2x b_g(x)+v_N(x),\qquad 0\leq v_N(x)\leq3C.             \tag{4}
\]
Here \(|g|\leq G+1\).  If \(x\leq g\), the service part of
\(2xb_g(x)\) is nonpositive.  If \(x>g\), its only possibly positive case
is bounded by
\(2\nu |g||x|\leq d x^2+\nu^2g^2/d\).  Thus
\[
 G_{1,N}x^2\leq-dx^2+\nu^2(G+1)^2/d+3C.                            \tag{5}
\]
Stationarity and \(d\geq2c\) yield
\(\sup_{N,p,\gamma}\mathbb E_{
ho_{1,N}}X_{1,N}^2<\infty\).
The same calculation without the service term treats the control arm.
Applying the jump binomial formula to \(x^{2r}\), absorbing its leading
term \(-2rdx^{2r}\) by Young's inequality, inductively gives
\[
 \sup_{N,p,\gamma}\mathbb E_{
ho_{\ell,N}}|X_{\ell,N}|^{2r}<\infty
 \quad(r\in\mathbb N,\ \ell=0,1).                                \tag{6}
\]
No limit assertion is used in (4)--(6).

For completeness, the invariant-law limit follows directly from detailed
balance.  Treatment weights satisfy
\[
 \frac{\rho_{1,N}(k+1)}{\rho_{1,N}(k)}
 =\frac{\lambda(N-k)}{\tau(k+1)+\nu\min(k+1,M_N)}.                 \tag{7}
\]
Uniformly for \(|x|\leq R\), the logarithm of (7) is
\[
 \delta\frac{b_g(x)}q+O_R(\delta^2).                              \tag{8}
\]
Indeed, expand both logarithms about the common positive value \(q\); the
map \(x\mapsto\min(x,g)\) is one-Lipschitz, so the same remainder applies
when \([x,x+\delta]\) crosses \(g\).  On the other hand the candidate
density obeys
\[
 q\{\log\pi_g\}'(x)=b_g(x)
\]
on the two sides of \(g\), with matching value and first derivative at
\(g\).  Hence (8), multiplication of ratios, and Riemann summation show
on each compact set that
\[
 \sup_{x_k\in E_{1,N}\cap[-R,R]}
 \left|\delta^{-1}\rho_{1,N}(k)-\pi_g(x_k)\right|\longrightarrow0. \tag{9}
\]
To justify the normalization in this ratio argument, first restrict to a
compact interval carrying all but \(O(R^{-2})\) mass by (5), normalize the
Riemann sums there, and then let \(R\to\infty\).  This also proves uniqueness
of the possible limit.  Formula (6) upgrades (9) to convergence of every
fixed polynomial moment.  In the control arm, detailed balance gives the
binomial law with success probability \(a_0\), and the same argument gives
the normal density \(\pi_0\).  Since \(g-\gamma\to0\), and the displayed
piecewise Gaussian densities are continuous in \((p,g)\) in weighted
\(L^1\), these conclusions are compact-uniform with limit \(\pi_\gamma\).

The drifts \(-dx\) and \(b_\gamma(x)\) are globally Lipschitz.  Equations
(3), (5), and the martingale decomposition of the coordinate imply compact
containment and the following stopping-time increment bound: for stopping times \(\sigma\) in a
fixed time interval and \(u\downarrow0\),
\[
 \mathbb E|X_{\ell,N}(\sigma+u)-X_{\ell,N}(\sigma)|^2
 \leq C(u+u^2).                                                    \tag{10}
\]
The stopping-time estimate (10), applied on dyadic partitions and combined
with Markov's inequality, gives tightness on every fixed time interval.
Every subsequential path limit therefore satisfies, by the compensated
generator identity and (3), the martingale problem for the displayed diffusion
generator.  Pathwise uniqueness follows from global Lipschitzness of the
drift, so the martingale problem is unique.  The stationary initial-law
limits in (9) identify the stationary solutions.  A contrary failure of
uniform bounded-Lipschitz convergence would supply a parameter sequence;
compactness supplies a convergent subsequence, to which (3)--(10) apply,
giving a contradiction.  This proves the two uniform stationary path
limits.

It remains to identify the Poisson solutions and energies.  For either
limiting diffusion, write \(b\), \(q_*\), \(\pi\), and
\(m=\int x\pi(x)\,dx\).  The stationary equation is
\(q_*\pi'=b\pi\).  With
\(F(x)=\int_{-\infty}^x(u-m)\pi(u)\,du\), the construction gives
\[
 q_*(\pi h')'=-F'=-(x-m)\pi,
 \qquad -\mathcal Lh=x-m.                                        \tag{11}
\]
Gaussian tails make the centering integral finite.  If two centered
solutions existed, their difference would be a centered harmonic function;
the zero stationary Dirichlet energy forces its derivative to vanish, hence
the difference is zero.

For the treatment diffusion, couple solutions started at \(y>x\) with the
same Brownian motion.  The secant slope of \(b_\gamma\) lies in
\([-D,-d]\), so order is preserved and
\[
 e^{-Dt}(y-x)\leq X_t^y-X_t^x\leq e^{-dt}(y-x).                    \tag{12}
\]
The resolvent representation
\(h(x)=\int_0^\infty\{\mathbb E_xX_t-m\}\,dt\), justified by (12),
then yields
\[
 \frac1D\leq h_\gamma'(x)\leq\frac1d.                            \tag{13}
\]
For the control, (11) gives \(h_0(x)=x/d\).  Integration by parts in
(11), with Gaussian boundary terms, gives
\[
 2\int(x-m)h(x)\pi(x)\,dx
   =2q_*\int\{h'(x)\}^2\pi(x)\,dx.                                \tag{14}
\]
Thus \(V_0=2q_0/d^2=2\lambda\tau/d^3\), and (14) is the stated formula
for \(V_\gamma\).

Finally we connect (14) to the exact finite systems.  For an arm with birth
rates \(B_k\), death rates \(D_k\), invariant weights \(\rho_k\), and
\(f_k=(k-\mathbb E K)/\sqrt N\), define
\[
 A_k=\sum_{i=0}^k\rho_i f_i,
 \qquad h_N(k+1)-h_N(k)=-\frac{A_k}{\rho_kB_k},
 \qquad \sum_k\rho_kh_N(k)=0.                                    \tag{15}
\]
Detailed balance telescopes (15) to \(-\mathcal A_Nh_N=f\), and its exact
stationary energy is
\[
 V_N=2\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\frac{A_k^2}{\rho_kB_k}.                    \tag{16}
\]
An ordered basic coupling of chains started one count apart loses its
discrepancy at a rate between \(d\) and \(D\): the missing-birth rate is
\(\lambda\), while the increment of the death rate lies between \(\tau\)
and \(\tau+\nu\).  The finite-chain resolvent consequently gives
\[
 0\leq h_N(k+1)-h_N(k)\leq\frac1{d\sqrt N}.                       \tag{17}
\]
On compact scaled intervals, (9), polynomial-moment convergence, and
(15) imply uniformly
\[
 \delta^{-1}\{h_N(k+1)-h_N(k)\}\longrightarrow h_\gamma'(x_k).  \tag{18}
\]
The energy contribution outside \([-R,R]\) is at most
\(3C d^{-2}\rho_N\{|X_N|>R\}\) by (17), and this tends uniformly to zero
as \(R\to\infty\) by (6).  Riemann summation of (16) on \([-R,R]\), then
letting \(R\to\infty\), proves
\[
 \sup_{p,|\gamma|\leq G}|V_{0,N}-V_0|\to0,
 \qquad
 \sup_{p,|\gamma|\leq G}|V_{1,N}-V_\gamma|\to0.                 \tag{19}
\]
Equations (3), (9)--(14), and (19) prove every assertion of the theorem.

All processes in this proof are stationary by the model-class definition.
For each arm let \(f_{\ell,N}=X_{\ell,N}-
\mathbb E X_{\ell,N}\), and let \(h_{\ell,N}\) be the exact centered
finite-chain solution constructed by the flux formula (15) in the diffusion
theorem.  Dynkin's identity is exact:
\[
 \int_0^{T_N}f_{\ell,N}(X_{\ell,N}(t))\,dt
 =M_{\ell,N}(T_N)-
   \{h_{\ell,N}(X_{\ell,N}(T_N))-h_{\ell,N}(X_{\ell,N}(0))\},     \tag{27}
\]
where \(M_{\ell,N}\) is a compensated jump martingale.  Consequently
\[
 \sqrt{NT_N}(\widehat\theta_N-\theta_N)
 =T_N^{-1/2}\{M_{0,N}(T_N)-M_{1,N}(T_N)\}+o_{\mathbb P}(1).        \tag{28}
\]
To justify the endpoint term uniformly, the gradient bound (17) makes
\(h_{\ell,N}\) \(1/d\)-Lipschitz in the scaled coordinate.  Centering and
the stationary second-moment bound then give
\(\sup\mathbb E h_{\ell,N}^2<\infty\), so division by \(\sqrt{T_N}\)
and the horizon-divergence assumption prove (28).

Let
\[
 U_{\lambda,N}=C_\lambda-\lambda E_\lambda,
 \quad U_{\tau,N}=C_\tau-\tau E_\tau,
 \quad U_{\nu,N}=C_\nu-\nu E_\nu.                               \tag{29}
\]
The marked-history and dynamics assumptions make these three orthogonal
counting-process martingales, with brackets
\(\lambda E_\lambda\), \(\tau E_\tau\), and \(\nu E_\nu\).  Stationary
means, (6), and the spectral-gap estimate below imply
\[
 \frac1{NT_N}(E_\lambda,E_\tau,E_\nu)
 \longrightarrow (s_\lambda,s_\tau,s_\nu)
 :=(2-a_0-a,a_0+a,a)                                             \tag{30}
\]
uniformly in probability.  Each component is bounded away from zero because
\(a_0,a,1-a_0,1-a\) are compact-uniformly positive.  Thus the fixed positive
fallbacks are used with probability tending to zero, and
\[
 \sqrt{NT_N}(\widehat p-p)_j
 =\frac{U_{j,N}/\sqrt{NT_N}}{E_j/(NT_N)}.                          \tag{31}
\]

We record why the time averages in (30), and all brackets below, concentrate
without any upper restriction on \(T_N/N\).  If
\(-\mathcal A_N\phi=\kappa\phi\) and
\(g_k=\phi(k+1)-\phi(k)\), subtraction at adjacent states gives
\[
 -\kappa g_k
 =B_{k+1}(g_{k+1}-g_k)+D_k(g_{k-1}-g_k)
  -\{B_k-B_{k+1}+D_{k+1}-D_k\}g_k.                               \tag{32}
\]
At a positive maximum of a nonzero discrete gradient, (32) implies
\(\kappa\geq B_k-B_{k+1}+D_{k+1}-D_k\geq\lambda+\tau=d\);
changing sign covers the other case.  Reversibility of a birth--death chain
therefore gives spectral gap at least \(d\).  For any bounded stationary
integrand \(r\), spectral decomposition then yields
\[
 \operatorname{Var}\left(T^{-1}\int_0^T r(K(t))\,dt\right)
 \leq\frac{2\operatorname{Var}_\rho(r)}{dT}.                      \tag{33}
\]
The normalized exposure and bracket integrands are uniformly bounded, so
(33) proves their concentration.

The predictable bracket of the first coordinate in (28) converges, by arm
independence and the energy convergence in the diffusion theorem, to
\(V_0+V_\gamma=V\).  The score-score block obtained from (29)--(31) is
\[
 \operatorname{diag}\left(\frac\lambda{s_\lambda},
                           \frac\tau{s_\tau},
                           \frac\nu{s_\nu}\right)=\Gamma.        \tag{34}
\]
It remains to compute the cross block rather than assume it vanishes.  A
control birth contributes limiting occupation-martingale coefficient
\(1/d\), and a treatment birth contributes \(-h_\gamma'(X)\).  Natural
recoveries contribute \(-1/d\) and \(+h_\gamma'(X)\), respectively;
a treatment service recovery contributes \(+h_\gamma'(X)\).  Detailed
balance, the local gradient limit (18), and tail domination by (17) therefore
give the un-divided cross-bracket rates
\[
\begin{split}
 c_\lambda&=\lambda\{(1-a_0)/d-(1-a)H\}=\lambda A_\lambda,\\
 c_\tau&=\tau\{-a_0/d+aH\}=\tau A_\tau,\\
 c_\nu&=\nu aH=\nu A_\nu.
\end{split}                                                       \tag{35}
\]
Division by the exposure limits in (31) turns (35) into
\(A^{\mathsf T}\Gamma\).  Equations (34)--(35) hence give exactly
\[
 \Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}V&A^{\mathsf T}\Gamma\\
                        \Gamma A&\Gamma\end{pmatrix}.             \tag{36}
\]

For clarity, the Gaussian step is also derived from primitives.  For every
fixed vector \(t\), apply Taylor's formula
\(e^{iu}=1+iu-u^2/2+o(u^2)\) conditionally at successive jumps of the
scalar martingale obtained by projecting (28)--(31) along \(t\).  Its
largest normalized jump is bounded by
\(C(1/\sqrt{NT_N}+1/\sqrt{T_NN})\), using (17), and therefore tends to
zero.  The sum of conditional quadratic terms is the predictable bracket,
which converges by (33) to \(t^{\mathsf T}\Sigma t\); the sum of the
Taylor remainders is bounded by the largest jump times the bracket and is
\(o_{\mathbb P}(1)\).  Iterated conditional expectation consequently gives
the characteristic function
\(\exp\{-t^{\mathsf T}\Sigma t/2\}\).  The same calculation after stopping
at a fixed bracket level supplies uniform integrability.  The
preceding characteristic-function identity for every vector \(t\) directly
identifies the centered multivariate Gaussian limit (36).

Compactness upgrades this to the stated uniform limit: from any allegedly
failing parameter sequence choose a convergent subsequence; (6), (17),
(19), and (30)--(35) apply with the same constants, while continuity of all
Gaussian integrals makes the comparison covariance converge, a
contradiction.

Finally, (31) implies uniform consistency of \(\widehat p\), and
\[
 \widehat\gamma_N-\gamma_N
 =-\sqrt N\{a(\widehat p)-a(p)\}=O_{\mathbb P}(T_N^{-1/2}).         \tag{37}
\]
The computational clipping to \([c/2,2C]^3\) is asymptotically inactive.
Continuity and the positive lower bound on \(V\) yield
\(\widehat V/V\to1\) uniformly.  Studentization of the first coordinate
of (36), followed by the continuity of the standard normal distribution,
proves
\[
 \sup_{p,|\gamma|\leq G}
 \left|\mathbb P_{p,\gamma}\{\theta_N\in I_{\mathrm{emp}}\}
       -(1-\alpha)\right|\to0.
\]
Because (27) is an exact prelimit identity, no comparison of paths over the
growing interval was made, and hence no upper relation between \(T_N\) and
\(N\) is required.

Let
\[
 \vartheta_N(p';M)=a_0(p')-a(p')-
 N^{-1/2}m_{p',\,(M-Na(p'))/\sqrt N}.                              \tag{38}
\]
Then the fitted-center definition says
\(\widetilde\theta_N=\vartheta_N(\widehat p;M_N)\).  The resolved
kink-residual theorem gives (26), and therefore
\[
 |\vartheta_N(p;M_N)-\theta_N|
 =N^{-1/2}|m_{p,\gamma_N}-\mathbb E_{
ho_{1,N}}X_{1,N}|
 \leq K_{\mathrm{res}}N^{-1}.                                    \tag{39}
\]

We derive the fixed-staffing derivative.  Put
\(H_+=\int_\gamma^\infty h_\gamma'(x)\pi_\gamma(x)\,dx\).
Differentiating the stationary identity
\(\pi_\gamma\mathcal L_\gamma=0\) and applying the resulting signed
measure to the Poisson solution gives
\[
 \partial_\gamma m_\gamma
 =\int (\partial_\gamma\mathcal L_\gamma)h_\gamma\,d\pi_\gamma
 =-\nu H_+.                                                       \tag{40}
\]
This differentiation is justified directly by the two Gaussian pieces and
their common boundary value; their derivatives have a common integrable
Gaussian envelope on the compact parameter and staffing set.  Differentiating
the Poisson equation in \(x\), using \(b_\gamma'=-D\) to the left and
\(-d\) to the right, and integrating against stationarity gives
\[
 D(H-H_+)+dH_+=1,
 \qquad D H-\nu H_+=1.                                           \tag{41}
\]
Combining (40)--(41) yields
\(\partial_\gamma m_\gamma=1-DH\).

In (38), \(M\) is held fixed, so
\(\nabla_p\{(M-Na(p))/\sqrt N\}=-\sqrt N\nabla a(p)\).  Hence
\[
 \nabla_p\vartheta_N(p;M_N)
 =\nabla a_0+(\partial_\gamma m_{p,\gamma_N}-1)\nabla a
   -N^{-1/2}\nabla_pm_{p,\gamma_N}
 =\nabla a_0-DH\nabla a+O(N^{-1/2}).                                \tag{42}
\]
The explicit Gaussian formulas make the omitted derivative uniformly
bounded.  Since
\[
 \nabla a_0=((1-a_0)/d,-a_0/d,0)^{\mathsf T},\qquad
 \nabla a=((1-a)/D,-a/D,-a/D)^{\mathsf T},                        \tag{43}
\]
(42) is precisely \(A+O(N^{-1/2})\).

The same Gaussian differentiation bounds the Hessian of (38) by
\(C\sqrt N\) on a fixed enlargement of the compact set.  The joint law
gives \(\widehat p-p=O_{\mathbb P}((NT_N)^{-1/2})\) uniformly, so Taylor's
formula, (39), and the fitted-horizon assumption imply
\[
\begin{split}
 \sqrt{NT_N}(\widetilde\theta_N-\theta_N)
 &=A^{\mathsf T}\sqrt{NT_N}(\widehat p-p)
   +O_{\mathbb P}(T_N^{-1/2})+O(\sqrt{T_N/N})\\
 &=A^{\mathsf T}R_N+o_{\mathbb P}(1).
\end{split}                                                       \tag{44}
\]
Together with the joint covariance in the uniform joint law, (44) gives
\[
 \sqrt{NT_N}(\widetilde\theta_N-\theta_N)
 \Rightarrow\mathcal N(0,A^{\mathsf T}\Gamma A)=\mathcal N(0,Q). \tag{45}
\]
Subtracting (44) from the empirical coordinate gives variance
\[
 \operatorname{Var}(S-A^{\mathsf T}R)
 =V+Q-2A^{\mathsf T}\Gamma A=V-Q=W,                               \tag{46}
\]
and proves the second asserted limit.

The variances are uniformly nondegenerate.  From \(H\geq1/D\),
\(A_\nu=aH>0\), so the service-score term alone gives a compact-uniform
positive lower bound for \(Q\).  Moreover, (46) is the limiting energy of
the occupation martingale after orthogonal projection onto the three marked
count martingales.  Its treatment service component contains
\[
 \nu a\int\{h_\gamma'(x)-H\}^2\pi_\gamma(x)\,dx.                  \tag{47}
\]
This is positive: if \(h_\gamma'\) were constant, the Poisson equation on
the two positive-mass sides of the finite kink would require that constant
to be both \(1/D\) and \(1/d\), impossible because \(\nu>0\).
Continuity of the Gaussian integrals and compactness turn (47) into a
uniform positive lower bound for \(W\).

Equations (37), (40)--(43), and continuity now give
\(\widehat Q/Q\to1\) uniformly.  Studentizing (45) proves
\[
 \sup_{p,|\gamma|\leq G}
 \left|\mathbb P_{p,\gamma}\{\theta_N\in I_{\mathrm{fit}}\}
       -(1-\alpha)\right|\to0.
\]
Finally, (39) contributes at most
\(K_{\mathrm{res}}\sqrt{T_N/N}\) after normalization.  Thus
\(T_N/N\to0\) is sufficient, and it is the weakest relation that this
order-only bound by itself can force to zero, exactly as claimed.

We first verify that the stated oracle is effective and sound, rather than
assuming its guarantees.  Write the treatment density as
\(\pi_\gamma(x)=Z_\gamma^{-1}e^{-U_\gamma(x)}\), with its additive
constant chosen so \(U_\gamma(x^*)=0\).  On its two quadratic pieces the
curvature lies between \(d/q\) and \(D/q\).  Consequently
\[
 U_\gamma(x)\geq\frac d{2q}(x-x^*)^2,
 \qquad
 Z_\gamma\geq\sqrt{\frac{2\pi q}{D}},
\]
and hence
\[
 \pi_\gamma(x)leq\sqrt{\frac D{2\pi q}}
 \exp\left\{-\frac d{2q}(x-x^*)^2\right\}.                       \tag{48}
\]
For rational \(R>|x^*|\), the elementary Gaussian tail inequality obtained
by integrating \(y e^{-dy^2/(2q)}/(R-|x^*|)\) gives
\[
 \mathbb P_{\pi_\gamma}(|X|>R)\leq B_R.                           \tag{49}
\]
The derivative bound \(h_\gamma'\leq1/d\) from the diffusion theorem then
gives
\[
 2q\int_{|x|>R}(h_\gamma')^2\pi_\gamma,dx
 \leq(2q/d^2)B_R.                                                 \tag{50}
\]
All coefficients in (48)--(50) have positive compact-uniform bounds by the
rate assumptions.  Increasing rational \(R\) therefore makes both rational
outward enclosures in (49)--(50) smaller than any prescribed rational
tolerance.

On \([-R,R]\), completing squares on each side of \(\gamma\) expresses
\(Z_\gamma\), \(m_\gamma\), and
\(F_\gamma(x)=\int_{-\infty}^x(u-m_\gamma)\pi_\gamma(u)\,du\)
using arithmetic, exponentials, and error functions.  Their power series,
after range reduction, have alternating or geometric rational remainder
bounds.  Since (48) also supplies a computable positive lower bound for
\(\pi_\gamma\) on a compact box, repeated rational interval subdivision,
split at the moving kink, encloses
\[
 V_\gamma=\frac2q\int_{-R}^R\frac{F_\gamma(x)^2}{\pi_\gamma(x)}\,dx
            +\text{the tail in (50)}                              \tag{51}
\]
with width tending to zero.  Bisection of the strictly increasing normal
distribution, using the same certified error-function evaluation, encloses
\(z_\alpha\).  Differentiation of the two Gaussian pieces under their
Gaussian envelope proves that \(V_\gamma\), and hence \(J(p,\gamma)\), is
continuously differentiable in \(\gamma\).  The same interval calculations
enclose \(|\partial_\gamma J|\) on the compact input box; outward rounding
the result upward gives a positive rational \(L_J\).  Subdivision in the
input name \(\mathfrak r(m)\), together with (49)--(51), therefore returns
a rational interval satisfying
\[
 J(p,\eta)\in\mathfrak O(I,m)\quad(\eta\in I),
 \qquad
 \operatorname{wid}\mathfrak O(I,m)
 \leq L_J\operatorname{diam}(I)+2^{-m},                           \tag{52}
\]
and point width at most \(2^{-m}\).  This proves the oracle properties from
the explicit Poisson representation and rational remainder bounds.

Assume first that \(G>0\).  Run the fair dyadic algorithm, using one
interval receipt and one midpoint point receipt for each visited interval.
Pruning is sound: if \(I\) contains a global minimizer \(\gamma^*\), its
lower receipt is at most \(J(p,\gamma^*)\), whereas every incumbent upper
receipt is at least the global minimum, so the strict pruning inequality can
never hold.  Thus all minimizers remain in the active cover.

At depth \(D_\epsilon\), every interval has diameter at most
\(2G2^{-D_\epsilon}\).  From the definitions of \(D_\epsilon\) and
\(m_\epsilon\),
\[
 L_J\operatorname{diam}(I)\leq\epsilon/4,
 \qquad 2^{-(m_\epsilon+D_\epsilon)}\leq\epsilon/8.                \tag{53}
\]
Thus each interval receipt has width at most \(3\epsilon/8\), and each
point receipt has width at most \(\epsilon/8\).  Let \(I^*\) be an active
interval containing a minimizer.  Its midpoint \(u^*\) satisfies, by the
Lipschitz certificate and (53),
\[
 J(p,u^*)\leq J(p,\gamma^*)+\epsilon/8.
\]
Therefore the incumbent obeys
\(U_\epsilon\leq J(p,\gamma^*)+\epsilon/4\).  Conversely, for every active
interval its lower receipt is at least the value of any enclosed point minus
its receipt width, hence at least
\(J(p,\gamma^*)-3\epsilon/8\).  Consequently
\[
 U_\epsilon-L_\epsilon\leq5\epsilon/8<\epsilon.                  \tag{54}
\]
Soundness of the receipts and the incumbent definition now give
\[
 L_\epsilon\leq\min_{|\gamma|\leq G}J(p,\gamma)
 \leq J(p,\gamma_\epsilon)\leq U_\epsilon,                        \tag{55}
\]
while the retained records, their statuses, and (54) have exactly the
semantics of \(\mathrm{Cert}\).

The full binary tree through depth \(D_\epsilon\) has
\(2^{D_\epsilon+1}-1\) nodes, which proves the interval-evaluation bound.
At most one interval and one point request are made per node, so the total is
less than \(2^{D_\epsilon+2}<3\cdot2^{D_\epsilon+1}\), all at precision at
least \(m_\epsilon\).  Pruning can only reduce these counts.  If \(G=0\),
the feasible set is a singleton and one point receipt directly supplies
(55) with the requested gap.  This proves termination, global optimality to
tolerance, and every certificate assertion without a convexity or uniqueness
assumption.

By the uniform energy convergence in the diffusion theorem and the common
positive lower bound on \(V_{0,N}+V_{1,N}\) and \(V_0+V_\gamma\), the
inequality
\[
 |\sqrt x-\sqrt y|\leq\frac{|x-y|}{\sqrt x+\sqrt y}
\]
implies
\[
 \Delta_N:=\sup_{p\in\mathcal P,\,|\gamma|\leq G}
 |J_N(p,\gamma)-J(p,\gamma)|\longrightarrow0.                    \tag{56}
\]
The capacity certificate gives
\(J(p,\gamma_\epsilon)-\inf_{|\gamma|\leq G}J(p,\gamma)\leq\epsilon\).
Adding and subtracting \(J\) and applying (56) yields, uniformly in \(p\),
\[
\begin{split}
 J_N(p,\gamma_\epsilon)-\inf_{|\gamma|\leq G}J_N(p,\gamma)
 &\leq J(p,\gamma_\epsilon)-\inf_{|\gamma|\leq G}J(p,\gamma)
      +2\Delta_N\\
 &\leq\epsilon+o(1),
\end{split}
\]
which is the claimed finite-system regret certificate.

Fix \(\lambda,\tau>0\) and take the continuous extension
\(\nu\downarrow0\).  Then \(D\to d\),
\(q=\lambda(\tau+\nu)/D\to\lambda\tau/d=q_0\), and, uniformly on compact
sets,
\[
 -dx-\nu\min(x,\gamma)\longrightarrow-dx.
\]
The two pieces of the displayed stationary density consequently coalesce
into \(\pi_0\); the Gaussian envelope (48) supplies dominated convergence.
Thus \(m_\gamma\to0\).  The flux formula (11), or the coupling bound followed
by dominated convergence in (14), gives \(h_\gamma'\to1/d\) and
\[
 V_\gamma\longrightarrow 2q_0/d^2
 =\frac{2\lambda\tau}{(\lambda+\tau)^3}.
\]

For the fixed-system reduction, hold \(N\) fixed.  The finite state chain is
irreducible by the positive-rate and staffing-interior conditions.  The
exact flux construction (15) solves the finite Poisson equation, and (27)
expresses the centered occupation integral as its jump martingale plus a
bounded endpoint.  As \(T_N\to\infty\), the finite-state ergodic theorem
makes the normalized predictable bracket converge to the exact energy
\(V_{\ell,N}\); bounded jumps make the conditional Taylor remainder vanish.
The scalar characteristic-function argument used in the uniform joint law
therefore gives the fixed-\(N\) occupation central limit theorem.  Its
generator, stationary target, Poisson solution, and energy are exactly those
of the stated finite-source model, so this is precisely the fixed-system
limit to which the cited Boutilier--Jonasson--Li--Yoeli occupation result
applies.  Hence both asserted sanity reductions follow.

theorem.statement:
There is a finite constant \(K_{\mathrm{res}}\), depending only on
\((c,C,G)\), such that for every \(N\geq N_0\),
\[
 \sup_{p\in\mathcal P,\,|\gamma|\leq G}
 \mathbb E_{\rho_{1,N}}
 \left|\{G_{1,N}-\mathcal L_{\gamma_N}\}
 h_{1,N}(X_{1,N})\right|
 \leq K_{\mathrm{res}}N^{-1/2}.
\]
This bound includes every state for which an available upward or downward
lattice jump crosses \(\gamma_N\).
theorem.proof_tex:
Set \(\delta=N^{-1/2}\) and \(g=\gamma_N\).  The diffusion theorem gives
\(1/D\leq h_g'\leq1/d\).  From the Poisson equation,
\[
 qh_g''(x)=-(x-m_g)-b_g(x)h_g'(x),
 \qquad b_g(x)=-dx-\nu\min(x,g).                                  \tag{20}
\]
The invariant second-moment bound proved there, applied also to the limiting
stationary equation, bounds \(|m_g|\) uniformly for
\(p\in\mathcal P\) and \(|g|\leq G+1\).  Hence
\[
 |h_g''(x)|\leq C_1(1+|x|).                                      \tag{21}
\]
On each open side of \(g\), differentiation of (20) gives
\[
 qh_g'''(x)=-1-b_g'(x)h_g'(x)-b_g(x)h_g''(x),                     \tag{22}
\]
where \(b_g'=-D\) to the left and \(b_g'=-d\) to the right.  Thus
\[
 |h_g'''(x)|\leq C_2(1+x^2)                                      \tag{23}
\]
away from the kink.  Because \(b_g\), \(h_g'\), and the right side of
(20) are continuous at \(g\), \(h_g''\) is continuous there.  Consequently
\(h_g''\) is locally absolutely continuous and (23) holds almost
everywhere.  Taylor's formula with integral remainder is therefore valid
on an interval crossing \(g\), not merely on intervals contained in one
smooth branch.

Let \(B_N(x)\) and \(D_N(x)\) denote the available up- and down-jump rates
at the state represented by \(x\).  Equations (1)--(2) in the diffusion
proof are exact, including at the physical endpoints because the unavailable
rate is zero.  Taylor expansion with (21)--(23) gives
\[
\begin{split}
 G_{1,N}h_g(x)
 &=b_g(x)h_g'(x)
   +\left[q+\frac\delta2\{(\tau-\lambda)x+
                 \nu\min(x,g)\}\right]h_g''(x)+R_N(x),\\
 |R_N(x)|
 &\leq \frac{\delta^3}{6}\{B_N(x)+D_N(x)\}
       \sup_{|u-x|\leq\delta}|h_g'''(u)|
 \leq C_3\delta(1+x^2).
\end{split}                                                       \tag{24}
\]
The second equality uses \(B_N+D_N\leq3CN\); it remains valid for a
kink-crossing jump by local absolute continuity.  The additional second
derivative term is, by (21), bounded in absolute value by
\(C_4\delta(1+x^2)\).  Subtracting
\(\mathcal L_gh_g=b_gh_g'+qh_g''\) from (24) yields the pointwise envelope
\[
 |(G_{1,N}-\mathcal L_g)h_g(x)|
 \leq C_5\delta(1+x^2).                                          \tag{25}
\]
The stationary drift calculation (4)--(5) in the diffusion proof gives
\(\sup_{N,p,\gamma}\mathbb E_{
ho_{1,N}}X_{1,N}^2<\infty\).
Taking stationary expectations in (25) proves the displayed bound with a
finite \(K_{\mathrm{res}}\).

As a consequence needed downstream, stationarity gives
\(\mathbb E_{
ho_{1,N}}G_{1,N}h_g(X_{1,N})=0\), whereas the Poisson
equation gives
\(\mathcal L_gh_g(x)=-(x-m_g)\).  Therefore (25) also proves
\[
 \left|\mathbb E_{
ho_{1,N}}X_{1,N}-m_{\gamma_N}\right|
 \leq K_{\mathrm{res}}N^{-1/2}.                                  \tag{26}
\]
This is the claimed order and is uniform over every ceiling phase.
